etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From いつ (itsu, “when”) + まで (made, “until, up to”) + も (mo, “even, also”, inclusive) Literally, "until even any time".
The construction itsu made ("until when") is attested already as Old Japanese itu made in the Man'yōshū of 759 CE. Likewise, the construction made mo ("even until") is also attested in the Man'yōshū, as is itu mo ("any time, whenever; always"). That said, the earliest attestation of the full phrase itsu made mo might not be until the Shaku Nihongi in the late 1200s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Reduplication of the archaic adverb いよ (iyo, “more and more, increasingly”), shift of いや (iya, “more and more, increasingly”), in turn from the prefix い (i-) and the adverb や (ya, “more and more, increasingly”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Onomatopoeia of the grunting noise made when straining oneself in effort.
The prefix usage appears in the Kanto region during the Edo period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From お (o, honorific marker) + 元気 (genki, “healthy”) + で (de, particle for location).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Gemination of きと (kito).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Negative of 済(す)む (sumu, “to finish; to be settled”), lit. "(the trouble) is not settled".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From どうして + も.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Dutch gom (“gum”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Persian قم (qom).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 不 (MC pjuw).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 五十(ごじゅう) (gojū, “fifty”) + 音(おん) (-on, “sound”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 差 is a daiyōji replacing 叉.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Found in the Man'yōshū, finished some time after 759 CE. Compare Middle Korean ᄇᆞᆯ〮 (pól, “field, plain”), whence modern 벌 (beol). Possibly from 原(はる) (haru) below, by vowel assimilation.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 原 (MC ngjwon, “source; origin; beginning”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Possibly related to 原(はら) (hara) or Middle Korean ᄇᆞᆯ〮 (pól, “field, plain”), whence modern 벌 (beol). The proximity of Kyūshū (where this pronunciation is prevalent) to the Korean Peninsula may support the latter connection.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨no₂mi₁ to₁⟩ → */nəmʲitʷo/ → /nomʉto//nomʉdo/ → /nondo/ → /nodo/
Shift from 喉(のんど) (nondo), ultimately from 喉(のみと) (nomito), a compound of 飲み (nomi, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 飲む (nomu), “to drink”) + 門 (to, “gate, door”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 喉 (huw).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/nomito/ > /nomto/ > /nomdo/ > /nondo/.
From 喉(のみと) (nomito).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 喉(のみと) (nomito).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 飲み (nomi, “drink”) + 門 (to, “passage”). Nomi is the nominalized form of the verb 飲む (nomu, “to drink”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appears from roughly the Muromachi period, superseding earlier to reading (see below). Likely a compound of either 背 (so, “back, behind”, ancient reading found in compounds) + 外 (to, “outside”), or 背 (so, “back, behind”, ancient reading found in compounds) + 所 (to, “place”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 外 (MC ngwajH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Listed in the Daijiten as being cognate with 切る (kiru, “to cut”), perhaps via ふ (fu, repetitive verb suffix). However, Samuel Martin thinks this is unlikely.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 密 (MC mit).
First cited to a text from 1092.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Literary Chinese 平等 (píngděng, “impartiality; unbiasedness; equality”). Originally a Buddhist term, hence the goon reading.
First cited to a text from 927.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū completed in 759 CE.
May be derived from 萎える (naeru, “to weaken; to wither; to bend; to become limp; to become listless”), from the classical form 萎ゆ (nayu) in the irrealis verb stem naya- + suppositional suffix む (mu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 所 (MC srjoX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₂ko₂ro₂⟩ → /tokoro/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *təkərə. Likely cognate with 床 (toko, “raised area; bed”).
A surface analysis suggests that this could be an ancient compound of ⟨to₂⟩ (Proto-Japonic *to (“place”), as in 跡 ⟨ato₂⟩, “footprint, track”, from “foot place, where one has stepped”) + ⟨ko₂⟩ (noun-forming suffixing element denoting “place”, as in ここ ⟨ko₂ko₂⟩, “here”, from “this place”) + ⟨ro₂⟩ (noun-forming suffixing element, apparently indicating within a general area, possibly as in 心 ⟨ko₂ko₂ro₂⟩, “heart, mind, emotions”, 頃 ⟨ko₂ro₂⟩, “general span of time, around a certain time”, うつろ ⟨uturo₂⟩, “hollowness, empty interior”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Listed in some sources as an abbreviation of tokoro above. However, this is also listed as cognate with 床 (toko, “raised area; bed”), which term already appears in use as far back as the Kojiki (712 CE), one of the oldest Japanese texts.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₁⟩ → /*tʷo/ → /to/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *to. Appears mainly as an affixing element indicating place, as in 後 (ato, “after; behind; the back of something”), from 跡 (ato, “footprint, track”), itself a compound of 足 (a, “foot”) + 所 (to, “place”); or in 留まる (todomaru, “to stop in a place”), itself a compound of と (to, “place”) + とまる (tomaru, “to stop”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with Japanese 掬う.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese 沿ふ (sopu). Used in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally the causative of 照(て)る (teru, “to shine”), from 照(て)ら (tera, the 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of 照(て)る (teru)) + す (-su, classical causative auxiliary, originally with 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”); modern せる (seru)), hence “to make shine”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨mawosu⟩ → */mawusu/ → /mausu/ → /mɔːsu/ → /moːsu/
Shift from Old Japanese 申す (mawosu), Late Old Japanese mausu.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/mausu/ → */maːsu/ → /masu/
Thought to be a shift from mōsu above, historical mausu.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 癥狀 (MC tring dzrjangH, “abdominal tumor, disease + form, appearance”)). Compare modern simplified Chinese 症状 (zhèngzhuàng, “symptom”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ana.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 職 (MC tsyik).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/pada/ → /ɸada/ → /hada/.
From Old Japanese, Proto-Japonic *panta. First attested in the Man'yōshū, completed sometime around 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Modern form of Old Japanese adjective よし (yoshi).
/joɕi/ (classical 終止形 (shūshikei) or terminal form) → /joki/ (classical 連体形 (rentaikei) or attributive form) → /joi/ (modern shūshikei and rentaikei)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Phonetic shift from the Old Japanese yoshi form of yoi above. Already in use as early as the Nihon Shoki, circa 720, then becoming common in eastern Japanese from the Edo period. This form is now obsolete, though it may still be found in some dialects.
/joɕi/ (classical 終止形 (shūshikei) or terminal form) → /eɕi/ (classical 終止形 (shūshikei) or terminal form) → /eki/ (classical 連体形 (rentaikei) or attributive form) → /ei/ (modern shūshikei and rentaikei)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Phonetic shift from ei above. This is now the most common form used in casual spoken Japanese.
/ei/ → /ii/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The usage of the character 這 is considered to be a 国訓 (kokkun) not derived from Chinese 漢文 (kanbun) tradition. Alongside China's usage of the character 這 /这 for a medieval pronoun, also of murky origins, this makes 這 a character with markedly different usages in both countries/languages. It is possibly a corrupt form of 𧥡, which is an ancient form of 誕 (MC danX) and borrowed as 蜒 (MC yen).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 速(そく) (soku, “fast”) + 力(りょく) (-ryoku, “power”)
